chapter: Ch 2 — Theory of Demand and Supply

questions.stem: In economics, the demand for a good means the quantity that a buyer is:

options.text: willing and able to buy at a given price in a given period
options.explanation: Correct. Demand is effective demand — desire backed by both the ability and the willingness to pay, stated at a price and over a period.

options.text: desires to own, whether or not able to pay for it
options.explanation: Desire without the ability to pay is only a want, not demand. Demand must be backed by purchasing power.
This describes consumption, not demand. Demand is the quantity buyers are willing and able to buy at each price.
Need is not the economic idea of demand. A buyer may need a good yet lack the means or willingness to buy it.

questions.sourceRef: Effective demand = desire + ability to pay + willingness to pay, at a price, over a period

questions.stem: The law of demand states that, other things remaining equal, price and quantity demanded:

options.explanation: Same-direction movement describes supply, not demand. The law of demand is an inverse relationship.
Correct. When price falls, quantity demanded rises, and when price rises, quantity demanded falls — an inverse relationship, ceteris paribus.
Price is the immediate influence on quantity demanded, so they are certainly related — inversely.

options.text: always change by the same proportion
options.explanation: Equal proportions describe unit elasticity, a special case. The law only states the direction, not the proportion.

questions.sourceRef: Law of demand: inverse relation between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus

questions.stem: The phrase 'other things remaining equal' (ceteris paribus) in the law of demand means that:

options.text: the price of the good is held constant
options.explanation: The price is exactly the thing that is allowed to change in the law of demand; it is the other influences that are held constant.
The clause is not about equality among buyers; it holds each buyer's income and the other determinants unchanged while the price varies.

options.text: income, tastes and related prices are held unchanged while price alone varies
options.explanation: Correct. Only the good's own price changes; income, tastes, prices of related goods and expectations are held constant.
Quantity demanded is the variable that responds; it is not held constant.

questions.sourceRef: Ceteris paribus holds all determinants but own price constant

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Demand · Why the curve slopes down
questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT help explain why the demand curve slopes downward?

options.text: The law of diminishing marginal utility
options.explanation: This does explain the downward slope: each extra unit is worth less, so more is bought only at a lower price.

options.text: The income effect of a price change
options.explanation: This does explain it: a price fall raises real purchasing power, part of which buys more of the good.

options.text: The substitution effect of a price change
options.explanation: This does explain it: a cheaper good draws buyers away from its substitutes.

options.text: A rise in the buyer's money income
options.explanation: Correct. A rise in income shifts the whole curve (a change in demand); it does not explain the downward slope of a single fixed curve.

questions.sourceRef: Diminishing MU, income effect and substitution effect explain the downward slope

questions.stem: Market demand for a good is obtained by:

options.text: adding the prices each buyer would pay
options.explanation: Market demand adds quantities, not prices. At each price we total the quantity demanded, not the price offered.

options.text: taking the average of individual demand curves
options.explanation: It is a sum, not an average. Averaging would understate the total quantity the market demands.

options.text: adding the quantities all buyers demand at each price (horizontal summation)
options.explanation: Correct. At every price we sum the quantities demanded by all buyers — horizontal summation of individual demand curves.

options.text: multiplying one buyer's demand by the price
options.explanation: That gives one buyer's spending, not the market quantity. Market demand sums quantities across buyers at each price.

questions.sourceRef: Market demand = horizontal sum of individual quantities at each price

questions.stem: Which of the following is a determinant of demand OTHER than the good's own price?

options.text: The quantity supplied of the good
options.explanation: Quantity supplied belongs to the supply side; it is not a determinant of the demand curve's position.

options.text: The slope of the demand curve
options.explanation: The slope is a property of the curve, not a determinant that shifts it.
The own price causes a movement along the curve, not a shift; the question asks for a determinant other than own price.
Correct. Income is a determinant of demand: a change in income shifts the whole demand curve (right for a normal good, left for an inferior good).

questions.sourceRef: Determinants: income, related prices, tastes, expectations, population

questions.stem: A fall in the good's own price, with everything else unchanged, causes a:

options.text: movement along the demand curve — a change in quantity demanded
options.explanation: Correct. A change in the good's own price moves the buyer along a fixed curve; a price fall is an extension (a change in quantity demanded).

options.text: rightward shift of the demand curve
options.explanation: A shift is caused by a change in a determinant other than own price. A change in own price does not shift the curve.

options.text: leftward shift of the demand curve
options.explanation: A leftward shift is a decrease in demand caused by another determinant, not by the good's own price falling.

options.text: change in demand at every price
options.explanation: A change in demand (the whole curve moving) comes from a non-price determinant, not from the own price changing.

questions.sourceRef: Own price change → movement along curve (change in quantity demanded)

questions.stem: An 'increase in demand' is best shown on a diagram as:

options.text: a downward movement along the same demand curve
options.explanation: A movement along the curve is a change in quantity demanded caused by the own price, not an increase in demand.

options.text: a rightward shift of the whole demand curve
options.explanation: Correct. An increase in demand means more is demanded at every price, shown by the entire curve shifting to the right.

options.text: a steepening of the demand curve
options.explanation: A change of slope is about elasticity, not an increase in demand. An increase shifts the curve rightward.

options.text: a leftward shift of the whole demand curve
options.explanation: A leftward shift is a decrease in demand — less demanded at every price — the opposite of an increase.

questions.sourceRef: Increase in demand = rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.stem: At a price of ₹ 15, three buyers demand 8, 14 and 23 units respectively. What is the market demand at ₹ 15?

options.explanation: This omits one buyer. Market demand adds the quantity of every buyer: 8 + 14 + 23.
This adds only two of the three buyers. All three quantities must be summed.
Correct. Market demand is the horizontal sum: 8 + 14 + 23 = 45 units at ₹ 15.
15 is the price, not a quantity. Market demand sums the three quantities, giving 45 units.

questions.sourceRef: Market demand = sum of individual quantities at the given price

questions.stem: A Giffen good is best described as:

options.text: a luxury bought to display status
options.explanation: That describes a Veblen or conspicuous good, not a Giffen good.

options.text: a good with many close substitutes
options.explanation: Close substitutes make demand elastic; this is unrelated to the Giffen exception.

options.text: an inferior good whose demand rises when its price rises, because the income effect outweighs the substitution effect
options.explanation: Correct. A Giffen good is a strongly inferior staple; a price rise makes the buyer poorer in real terms, and the negative income effect dominates, raising quantity demanded.

options.text: a good whose price never changes
options.explanation: A Giffen good is defined by its unusual response to a price change, not by a fixed price.

readLink.label: Read: Exceptions to the law of demand, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: Giffen good: inferior good, income effect outweighs substitution effect

questions.stem: Diamonds and premium brands bought partly to display status, whose demand can rise as their price rises, are examples of:

options.explanation: Giffen goods are inferior staples, not status luxuries. The status motive points to Veblen goods.
Complements are goods used together; this has nothing to do with the status motive described.
Perfect elasticity is a shape of the demand curve, not the status-driven exception described.
Correct. Veblen (conspicuous) goods are luxuries whose high price signals prestige, so demand can rise with price.

readLink.label: Read: Exceptions to the law of demand, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: Veblen/conspicuous goods: price signals status, demand can rise with price

questions.stem: During a rising share market, investors buy more shares as prices climb because they expect prices to rise further. This is an exception to the law of demand arising from:

options.text: the diminishing marginal utility of shares
options.explanation: Diminishing marginal utility supports the law of demand, not the exception. The buying here is driven by expectations.
Inferior goods relate to the Giffen exception, not to buying more in expectation of further price rises.

options.text: expectations of a further rise in price (speculation)
options.explanation: Correct. When buyers expect the price to keep rising, they buy more now to beat the increase — a speculative exception to the law of demand.
Complementarity is about goods used together; it does not explain buying more as prices rise.

readLink.label: Read: Exceptions to the law of demand, §5 →

questions.sourceRef: Speculative demand: expectation of further price rise raises current purchases

questions.stem: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, as a person consumes more units of a good:

options.text: the marginal utility of each successive unit falls
options.explanation: Correct. Each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the one before, which is why a buyer will pay less for it.

options.text: total utility falls with every unit
options.explanation: Total utility keeps rising while marginal utility is positive; it falls only once marginal utility turns negative.

options.text: the marginal utility of each unit rises
options.explanation: Rising marginal utility would contradict the law; the law says marginal utility falls as consumption grows.
Constant marginal utility is not the law of diminishing marginal utility, which requires marginal utility to fall.

readLink.label: Read: The utility basis of demand, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Marginal utility falls as more of a good is consumed

questions.stem: Consumer surplus is defined as:

options.text: the amount a buyer actually pays for a good
options.explanation: That is the buyer's expenditure, not the surplus. Surplus is the excess of value over the amount paid.

options.text: the excess of what a buyer is willing to pay over what the buyer actually pays
options.explanation: Correct. Consumer surplus is the gap between the maximum a buyer would have paid and the price actually paid.

options.text: the profit earned by the seller
options.explanation: Seller profit is a producer-side concept; consumer surplus is a benefit to the buyer.

options.text: the total utility of the good in utils
options.explanation: Consumer surplus is measured in money, as willingness to pay minus amount paid, not in utils of total utility.

questions.sourceRef: Consumer surplus = willingness to pay − amount actually paid

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Utility · TU and MU relationship
questions.stem: Total utility is at its maximum when marginal utility is:

options.explanation: Total utility is still rising when marginal utility is at its highest; it is not yet at a maximum.
While marginal utility is positive, total utility is still increasing, so it has not reached its maximum.
Correct. When marginal utility is zero, one more unit adds nothing, so total utility is at its peak (the point of satiation).
When marginal utility is negative, total utility is already falling — past its maximum, not at it.

readLink.label: Read: The utility basis of demand, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: TU is maximum when MU = 0

questions.stem: Spending on two goods X and Y, a consumer is in equilibrium (cardinal approach) when:

options.text: the prices of X and Y are equal
options.explanation: Equal prices are not required. Equilibrium balances marginal utility per rupee, not the prices themselves.

options.text: the marginal utilities of X and Y are equal
options.explanation: Equal marginal utilities are not enough unless the prices are equal too. The rule equalises marginal utility per rupee.

options.text: the total utilities of X and Y are equal
options.explanation: Equilibrium is a marginal condition, not a matter of equal total utilities.

options.text: the marginal utility per rupee is equal across the two goods (MUx ÷ Px = MUy ÷ Py)
options.explanation: Correct. The law of equi-marginal utility: the consumer allocates spending so the marginal utility per rupee is the same for every good.

readLink.label: Read: The utility basis of demand, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Equi-marginal utility: MUx/Px = MUy/Py

questions.stem: Which property of indifference curves is correct?

options.text: They slope upward from left to right
options.explanation: Indifference curves slope downward: to keep satisfaction constant, more of one good must be offset by less of the other.

options.text: They are concave to the origin
options.explanation: They are convex to the origin, reflecting a diminishing marginal rate of substitution.
Correct. Two indifference curves cannot intersect, because a single bundle cannot give two different levels of satisfaction.

options.text: A higher curve represents lower satisfaction
options.explanation: A higher curve (further from the origin) represents higher satisfaction, because it holds more of both goods.

questions.sourceRef: Indifference curves: downward-sloping, convex, non-intersecting, higher = better

questions.stem: In the indifference-curve approach, the consumer is in equilibrium at the point where:

options.text: the budget line crosses the lowest indifference curve
options.explanation: Crossing a low curve is not optimal; the consumer can reach a higher curve within the same budget.

options.text: the highest indifference curve on the map is reached, regardless of the budget
options.explanation: The consumer is limited by the budget line and cannot reach curves beyond it. Equilibrium is the highest curve the budget can touch.
Indifference curves never intersect, so this cannot describe equilibrium.

options.text: the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve
options.explanation: Correct. Equilibrium is the tangency point, where the marginal rate of substitution equals the price ratio and the consumer reaches the highest affordable curve.

questions.sourceRef: Ordinal equilibrium: budget line tangent to highest attainable indifference curve

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · Price elasticity from percentages
questions.stem: A 10% rise in the price of a good causes a 25% fall in the quantity demanded. The price elasticity of demand (in magnitude) is:

options.explanation: 0.4 is the ratio the wrong way up (10 ÷ 25). Elasticity is percentage change in quantity over percentage change in price.
Correct. e = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5 in magnitude — elastic demand.
This is not the ratio of the two percentages. 25 ÷ 10 gives 2.5, not 2.
0.25 confuses the percentages with the elasticity. The elasticity is 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5.

questions.sourceRef: e = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · Percentage method from actuals
questions.stem: The price of a good rises from ₹ 20 to ₹ 25 and the quantity demanded falls from 400 to 340 units. Using the percentage method on the original values, the price elasticity of demand (in magnitude) is:

options.explanation: 1.67 inverts the ratio. Here %ΔQ = 15% and %ΔP = 25%, so e = 15 ÷ 25, not 25 ÷ 15.
0.75 would come from a 15% quantity change against a 20% price change. The price change is 5 on 20 = 25%.
0.4 uses the wrong base for one change. %ΔQ = 60 ÷ 400 = 15%, %ΔP = 5 ÷ 20 = 25%.

questions.sourceRef: Percentage method: %ΔQ and %ΔP from original values

questions.stem: The price rises from ₹ 8 to ₹ 12 and the quantity demanded falls from 200 to 120 units. Using the arc method (average base), the price elasticity of demand (in magnitude) is:

options.explanation: 0.8 inverts the ratio of proportionate changes. The quantity term (80 ÷ 320 = 0.25) is divided by the price term (4 ÷ 20 = 0.20).
Unit elasticity would need equal proportionate changes. Here 0.25 ÷ 0.20 = 1.25, not 1.
Correct. Arc e = (80 ÷ 320) ÷ (4 ÷ 20) = 0.25 ÷ 0.20 = 1.25 — elastic over this arc.
0.5 does not match the averaged proportions. The correct arc figure is 0.25 ÷ 0.20 = 1.25.

questions.sourceRef: Arc e = (ΔQ ÷ (Q1+Q2)) ÷ (ΔP ÷ (P1+P2))

questions.stem: If the price elasticity of demand for a good is 0.6 (in magnitude), demand for the good is:

options.explanation: Correct. A magnitude below 1 means quantity responds proportionately less than price — inelastic demand.
Elastic demand needs a magnitude above 1. 0.6 is below 1, so demand is inelastic.
Unit elasticity is exactly 1. 0.6 is below 1, so demand is inelastic, not unit elastic.
Perfect elasticity is infinity. 0.6 is a finite value below 1 — inelastic demand.

readLink.label: Read: The five degrees of elasticity, §11 →

questions.sourceRef: e < 1 means inelastic

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · Point method from equation
questions.stem: For the demand equation Q = 300 − 6P, the price elasticity of demand at P = 20 (in magnitude) is:

options.explanation: 1.5 inverts the point-formula ratio. The correct value is 6 × (20 ÷ 180) = 2/3.
0.33 uses the wrong quantity or price. With Q = 180, e = 6 × 20 ÷ 180 = 2/3 ≈ 0.67.
2.0 does not follow from the point formula here. The elasticity is 120 ÷ 180 = 2/3.

questions.sourceRef: Point e = |slope| × (P ÷ Q); slope of Q = a − bP is b

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · New quantity from elasticity
questions.stem: The price elasticity of demand for a good is 2 (in magnitude). Its price rises by 10% from a level at which 800 units are sold. The new quantity demanded is:

options.explanation: A price rise lowers quantity demanded, so the new figure must be below 800, not above it.
Correct. %ΔQ = e × %ΔP = 2 × 10% = 20% fall; new quantity = 800 × (1 − 0.20) = 640 units.
720 is a 10% fall, which ignores the elasticity of 2. The quantity falls by 2 × 10% = 20%.
160 is the size of the fall (20% of 800), not the new quantity. The new quantity is 800 − 160 = 640.

questions.sourceRef: %ΔQ = e × %ΔP; new quantity = old × (1 − %ΔQ)

questions.stem: When the price of a good is cut from ₹ 40 to ₹ 30, the quantity sold rises from 500 to 800 units. Total revenue:

options.explanation: Correct. TR before = 40 × 500 = ₹ 20,000; TR after = 30 × 800 = ₹ 24,000; the increase is ₹ 4,000 — so demand is elastic.
TR rose, not fell. 24,000 is greater than 20,000, an increase of ₹ 4,000.
₹ 20,000 is the original total revenue, not the change. The change is 24,000 − 20,000 = ₹ 4,000.
Unchanged revenue would mean unit elasticity. Here revenue rose by ₹ 4,000, so demand is elastic.

questions.sourceRef: TR = P × Q; compare before and after

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · Elasticity from revenue behaviour
questions.stem: A shopkeeper raises the price of an item and finds that total revenue rises. Demand for the item is:

options.explanation: For elastic demand a price rise LOWERS total revenue. Rising revenue on a price rise means inelastic demand.
Correct. When a price rise raises total revenue, the quantity lost is proportionately small — demand is inelastic (e < 1).
With unit elasticity, total revenue would stay unchanged after a price change, not rise.
With perfectly elastic demand a price rise would lose all sales and revenue would collapse, not rise.

questions.sourceRef: Price rise + TR rise → inelastic demand

questions.stem: A buyer's income rises by 20% and the quantity demanded of a good rises by 30%. The income elasticity of demand is:

options.explanation: 0.67 inverts the ratio (20 ÷ 30). Income elasticity is %ΔQ ÷ %ΔincomeI = 30 ÷ 20.
The sign is wrong. Quantity rose as income rose, so the income elasticity is positive, +1.5.
2.5 is not 30 ÷ 20. The correct income elasticity is +1.5.
Correct. Income elasticity = 30 ÷ 20 = +1.5 — a positive value above 1 marks a normal good and a luxury.

questions.sourceRef: Income elasticity = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔIncome, sign kept

questions.stem: A household's income rises from ₹ 16,000 to ₹ 20,000 while its demand for a coarse grain falls from 40 kg to 34 kg. The income elasticity of demand is:

options.explanation: The sign is wrong. Quantity FELL as income rose, so the income elasticity is negative.
−1.67 inverts the ratio. %ΔQ = 15% fall and %ΔincomeI = 25% rise, so e = −15 ÷ 25, not −25 ÷ 15.
Correct. %ΔQ = 6 ÷ 40 = 15% fall; %ΔincomeI = 4,000 ÷ 16,000 = 25% rise; e = −15 ÷ 25 = −0.6 — an inferior good.
−0.15 is the quantity fraction alone, not divided by the income change. The elasticity is −15 ÷ 25 = −0.6.

questions.sourceRef: Negative income elasticity → inferior good

questions.stem: When the price of tea rises by 20%, the quantity of coffee demanded rises by 10%. The cross elasticity of demand for coffee with respect to the price of tea is:

options.explanation: The sign is wrong. Coffee demand rose when tea's price rose, so the cross elasticity is positive — substitutes.
Correct. Cross elasticity = +10 ÷ +20 = +0.5; the positive sign means tea and coffee are substitutes.
+2.0 inverts the ratio (20 ÷ 10). Cross elasticity is %ΔQ of coffee ÷ %ΔP of tea = 10 ÷ 20.
+0.4 is not 10 ÷ 20. The correct value is +0.5, marking substitutes.

questions.sourceRef: Positive cross elasticity → substitutes

questions.stem: When the price of a printer rises by 10%, the quantity of its ink cartridges demanded falls by 25%. The cross elasticity of demand for cartridges with respect to the printer's price is:

options.explanation: Correct. Cross elasticity = −25 ÷ +10 = −2.5; the negative sign means printers and cartridges are complements.
The sign is wrong. Cartridge demand fell when the printer's price rose, so the cross elasticity is negative — complements.
−0.4 inverts the ratio (10 ÷ 25). Cross elasticity is %ΔQ of cartridges ÷ %ΔP of printer = 25 ÷ 10.
−0.25 is the quantity fraction alone. Dividing the 25% fall by the 10% rise gives −2.5.

questions.sourceRef: Negative cross elasticity → complements

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · Sign of cross elasticity
questions.stem: A negative cross elasticity of demand between two goods indicates that the goods are:

options.explanation: Substitutes have a POSITIVE cross elasticity; a rise in one price raises demand for the other.
Unrelated goods have a cross elasticity of zero, not a negative value.
Correct. A negative cross elasticity means a rise in one good's price lowers demand for the other — they are complements.
Inferior refers to income elasticity, not cross elasticity. A negative cross elasticity marks complements.

questions.sourceRef: Cross elasticity: positive = substitutes, negative = complements, zero = unrelated

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Elasticity · Elasticity along a straight line
questions.stem: Along a straight-line (linear) demand curve, the price elasticity of demand:

options.text: is the same at every point
options.explanation: Although the slope is constant, elasticity is not: it depends on the price-to-quantity ratio, which changes along the line.
Elasticity is zero only for a vertical line. A downward-sloping straight line has different elasticities along it.
Infinite elasticity belongs to a horizontal line, not a downward-sloping straight-line demand curve.

options.text: varies from point to point, being higher at higher prices
options.explanation: Correct. On a linear demand curve elasticity falls as you move down it: it is greater than 1 in the upper (high-price) part, 1 at the midpoint, and less than 1 in the lower part.

questions.sourceRef: Point e = |slope| × P/Q varies along a straight line even though slope is constant

questions.stem: When the price of a good falls from ₹ 12 to ₹ 10, the quantity demanded rises from 250 to 300 units. Using the percentage method on the original values, the price elasticity of demand (in magnitude) is:

options.explanation: 0.83 inverts the ratio. %ΔQ = 20% and %ΔP = 16.67%, so e = 20 ÷ 16.67, not the reverse.
Unit elasticity would need equal proportionate changes. Here quantity changes more than price, so e is above 1.
2.4 is not the ratio of the two percentages. 20 ÷ 16.67 gives 1.2.

questions.sourceRef: Percentage method from original values

questions.stem: A good whose income elasticity of demand is greater than 1 is classified as:

options.explanation: Inferior goods have a NEGATIVE income elasticity. A value above 1 is positive and marks a luxury.
Giffen goods relate to a price-demand anomaly, not to income elasticity above 1.
Correct. A positive income elasticity above 1 means demand rises faster than income — the mark of a luxury.
A necessity has an income elasticity between 0 and 1. Above 1 the good is a luxury.

questions.sourceRef: Income elasticity > 1 → luxury; 0 to 1 → necessity; < 0 → inferior

questions.stem: Demand for a good tends to be MORE price-elastic when:

options.text: the good is a basic necessity
options.explanation: Necessities have inelastic demand — they are bought whatever the price. This makes demand less elastic, not more.

options.text: the good takes only a tiny share of the buyer's budget
options.explanation: A trifling budget share makes demand LESS elastic, because a price change is barely felt.

options.text: the good has no close substitutes
options.explanation: With no substitutes buyers cannot switch away, so demand is inelastic. Elastic demand needs available substitutes.

options.text: the good has many close substitutes
options.explanation: Correct. The more (and closer) the substitutes, the more elastic the demand, because buyers switch away easily when the price rises.

questions.sourceRef: More/closer substitutes → more elastic demand

questions.stem: The law of supply states that, other things remaining equal, price and quantity supplied:

options.explanation: Opposite-direction movement describes demand. Supply moves in the same direction as price.
Correct. A higher price makes production more profitable and draws out more output, so quantity supplied rises with price — a direct relationship.
Price is the immediate influence on quantity supplied, so they are directly related.
Equal proportions describe unit elasticity of supply, a special case, not the general law.

readLink.label: Read: Supply — the law and the curve, §15 →

questions.sourceRef: Law of supply: direct relation between price and quantity supplied

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Supply · Elasticity of supply from percentages
questions.stem: The quantity supplied of a good rises by 30% when its price rises by 12%. The price elasticity of supply is:

options.explanation: Correct. Elasticity of supply = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP = 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5 — an elastic supply.
0.4 inverts the ratio (12 ÷ 30). Elasticity of supply is %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP = 30 ÷ 12.
3.6 is not 30 ÷ 12. The correct elasticity of supply is 2.5.
1.5 is not the ratio of the two percentages. 30 ÷ 12 gives 2.5.

questions.sourceRef: Elasticity of supply = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Supply · Elasticity of supply from actuals
questions.stem: The price of a good rises from ₹ 50 to ₹ 60 and the quantity supplied rises from 300 to 345 units. The price elasticity of supply is:

options.explanation: 1.33 inverts the ratio. %ΔQs = 15% and %ΔP = 20%, so e = 15 ÷ 20, not 20 ÷ 15.
1.5 does not follow from these percentages. %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75.
Correct. %ΔQs = 45 ÷ 300 = 15%; %ΔP = 10 ÷ 50 = 20%; elasticity of supply = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75 — inelastic supply.
0.6 uses a wrong base for one change. The correct value is 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75.

questions.sourceRef: Elasticity of supply from actual values

questions.stem: A fall in the price of a raw material used to make a good will:

options.text: cause a movement up along the supply curve
options.explanation: A movement along the supply curve is caused by the good's OWN price, not by a change in input costs.
Lower input costs change supply at every price, so the curve does move — it does not stay put.

options.text: shift the supply curve to the left
options.explanation: Lower costs INCREASE supply, shifting the curve right, not left.

options.text: shift the supply curve to the right (an increase in supply)
options.explanation: Correct. Cheaper inputs lower costs and raise the quantity offered at every price — an increase in supply, a rightward shift.

readLink.label: Read: Supply — the law and the curve, §15 →

questions.sourceRef: Lower input cost → increase in supply → rightward shift

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Supply · Slope of the supply curve
questions.stem: The supply curve typically slopes upward from left to right because:

options.text: buyers demand more when the price is high
options.explanation: This is about demand, not supply. The supply curve's slope concerns sellers, not buyers.

options.text: marginal utility falls as more is consumed
options.explanation: Diminishing marginal utility explains the downward demand curve, not the upward supply curve.

options.text: a higher price makes production more profitable, drawing out more output
options.explanation: Correct. As price rises, producing more becomes profitable, so sellers offer a larger quantity — the direct price-quantity relation of supply.
This does not explain the supply curve's slope, which follows from the profitability of extra output at higher prices.

readLink.label: Read: Supply — the law and the curve, §15 →

questions.sourceRef: Upward supply curve: higher price → more profitable output → more supplied

questions.stem: A supply curve drawn as a vertical straight line represents supply that is:

options.explanation: Correct. A vertical supply curve means the quantity supplied does not change at all with price — the fixed supply of a rare item or the very short run.
Perfectly elastic supply is a HORIZONTAL line, not a vertical one.
Unit-elastic supply is not vertical; a vertical line means zero elasticity.
A vertical line is the opposite of elastic — its elasticity is zero.

questions.sourceRef: Vertical supply curve = perfectly inelastic (e = 0)

questions.stem: An 'increase in supply' means that:

options.text: more is supplied because the good's own price rose
options.explanation: That is a movement along the supply curve (an extension), not an increase in supply. An increase in supply is a shift.

options.text: more is supplied at every price — the whole curve shifts right
options.explanation: Correct. An increase in supply is a rightward shift of the entire curve, so a greater quantity is offered at each and every price.

options.text: less is supplied at every price
options.explanation: Less at every price is a DECREASE in supply, a leftward shift — the opposite of an increase.
A change of slope is about elasticity, not an increase in supply, which is a rightward shift.

readLink.label: Read: Supply — the law and the curve, §15 →

questions.sourceRef: Increase in supply = rightward shift of the supply curve

questions.stem: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 − 4P and the supply is Qs = 6P − 100, with P in rupees. The equilibrium price is:

options.explanation: At ₹ 20, Qd = 120 and Qs = 20, which are not equal. Setting Qd = Qs gives P = 30.
Correct. Set 200 − 4P = 6P − 100 → 300 = 10P → P = 30, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
At ₹ 50, Qd = 0 and Qs = 200 — a large surplus, not equilibrium. The market clears at P = 30.
At ₹ 10, Qd = 160 but Qs = −40 (no supply). Equilibrium is where the two are equal, at P = 30.

questions.sourceRef: Equilibrium: set Qd = Qs, solve for P

questions.stem: The demand for a good is Qd = 200 − 4P and the supply is Qs = 6P − 100. The equilibrium quantity is:

options.explanation: Correct. Equilibrium price is P = 30; substitute into demand: 200 − 4(30) = 80 units, and supply confirms 6(30) − 100 = 80.
120 is the quantity demanded at P = 20, not at the equilibrium price of 30. The equilibrium quantity is 80.
60 does not satisfy both equations at the equilibrium price. Substituting P = 30 gives 80 units.
100 is not the equilibrium quantity. At P = 30 both demand and supply give 80 units.

questions.sourceRef: Equilibrium quantity: substitute equilibrium price into either equation

questions.stem: In a market with demand Qd = 500 − 10P and supply Qs = 40P − 500, the equilibrium quantity is:

options.explanation: 200 does not satisfy both equations at the equilibrium price. Solving Qd = Qs gives P = 20 and quantity 300.
250 is not the equilibrium quantity here. At P = 20 both curves give 300 units.
500 is the demand intercept, not the equilibrium quantity. Substituting P = 20 gives 300 units.

questions.sourceRef: Solve Qd = Qs for P, then compute quantity

questions.stem: In a market with demand Qd = 1200 − 3P and supply Qs = 2P − 300, the equilibrium price is:

options.explanation: At ₹ 150 the two quantities are not equal. Setting Qd = Qs gives P = 300.
At ₹ 250, Qd = 450 and Qs = 200, not equal. The market clears at P = 300.
Correct. Set 1200 − 3P = 2P − 300 → 1,500 = 5P → P = 300, where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (both 300 units).
At ₹ 500, Qd = −300 (no demand). Equilibrium is where the two quantities are equal, at P = 300.

questions.sourceRef: Equilibrium: set Qd = Qs, solve for P

questions.stem: A market has Qd = 200 − 4P and Qs = 6P − 100 (equilibrium price ₹ 30). Demand now rises by 50 units at every price, so Qd = 250 − 4P. The new equilibrium price is:

options.explanation: ₹ 30 was the OLD equilibrium. A rightward demand shift raises the equilibrium price above 30.
Correct. Set 250 − 4P = 6P − 100 → 350 = 10P → P = 35, up from ₹ 30 — a demand increase raises price and quantity.
₹ 40 overstates the rise. Solving the new equilibrium gives P = 35, not 40.
₹ 25 is below the old price, but a demand increase raises the price. The new equilibrium is ₹ 35.

questions.stem: A market has Qd = 200 − 4P and Qs = 6P − 100 (equilibrium price ₹ 30). Supply now rises by 50 units at every price, so Qs = 6P − 50. The new equilibrium price is:

options.explanation: Correct. Set 200 − 4P = 6P − 50 → 250 = 10P → P = 25, down from ₹ 30 — a supply increase lowers the price and raises the quantity.
₹ 30 was the OLD equilibrium. A rightward supply shift lowers the equilibrium price below 30.
₹ 35 would follow a demand increase, not a supply increase. A supply increase lowers price to ₹ 25.
₹ 20 overstates the fall. Solving the new equilibrium gives P = 25, not 20.

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Equilibrium · Surplus at a high price
questions.stem: With demand Qd = 200 − 4P and supply Qs = 6P − 100 (equilibrium price ₹ 30), what exists in the market at a price of ₹ 40?

options.explanation: A shortage occurs below equilibrium. At ₹ 40, above the equilibrium of ₹ 30, supply exceeds demand — a surplus, not a shortage.
Correct. At ₹ 40, Qd = 200 − 160 = 40 and Qs = 240 − 100 = 140; supply exceeds demand by 100 units — a surplus that pushes the price down.
The gap is Qs − Qd = 140 − 40 = 100 units, not 60. The surplus is 100 units.

options.text: Neither — the market is in equilibrium
options.explanation: Equilibrium is at ₹ 30. At ₹ 40 the quantities differ, so there is a surplus of 100 units.

questions.sourceRef: Above equilibrium: Qs > Qd → surplus = Qs − Qd

questions.topic: Ch 2 · Equilibrium · Effect of a demand increase
questions.stem: Other things equal, an increase in demand (a rightward shift of the demand curve) will cause the equilibrium:

options.text: price to rise and quantity to fall
options.explanation: A demand increase moves price and quantity the SAME way; both rise, not in opposite directions.

options.text: price to fall and quantity to rise
options.explanation: Falling price with rising quantity describes a SUPPLY increase, not a demand increase.

options.text: price to fall and quantity to fall
options.explanation: Both falling describes a DECREASE in demand, not an increase.

options.text: price to rise and quantity to rise
options.explanation: Correct. A rightward demand shift raises both the equilibrium price and the equilibrium quantity — a demand shift moves the two together.
